question: What model architecture do the authors propose?
ground_truth: The Transformer, a network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
answer:
The authors propose the Transformer, a novel sequence transduction model architecture that relies entirely on self-attention, dispensing with recurrent or convolutional layers entirely (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 2, 4).

Key features of the architecture include:

Encoder-Decoder Structure: It follows an encoder-decoder setup using stacked self-attention and point-wise fully connected layers (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 3).
Encoder Stack: Composed of 6 identical layers, each containing a multi-head self-attention mechanism followed by a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 3).
Decoder Stack: Also composed of 6 identical layers, with an additional sub-layer that performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack, alongside masked self-attention to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 3, 4).
Attention Mechanisms: Utilizes scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention, allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
Position Embeddings: Since it lacks recurrence or convolutions, it adds "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks to give the model information about the relative or absolute position of tokens in the sequence (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 5).

question: What is the formula for scaled dot-product attention?
ground_truth: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.
answer:
The formula for scaled dot-product attention is:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Where:

$Q$ represents the matrix of queries (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
$K$ represents the matrix of keys (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
$V$ represents the matrix of values (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
$d_k$ is the dimension of the keys (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

question: Why are the dot products scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k)?
ground_truth: For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; scaling counteracts this.
answer:
The dot products are scaled by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ to prevent the softmax function from entering regions with extremely small gradients (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

Here is why this happens:

Growth in Variance: If the components of query $q$ and key $k$ are independent random variables with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, their dot product grows larger in magnitude as the dimension $d_k$ increases, resulting in a variance of $d_k$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).
Vanishing Gradients: For large values of $d_k$, these large dot product values push the softmax function into areas where its gradients become extremely small, slowing down or halting effective training (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ brings the variance back down to 1, stabilizing the gradients (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 4).

question: How many attention heads does the base model use and what are d_k and d_v?
ground_truth: h = 8 heads, with d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64.
answer:
The base model uses 8 parallel attention heads ($h = 8$) (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 5).

The query/key dimension ($d_k$) and the value dimension ($d_v$) are both 64 (calculated as $d_{\text{model}} / h = 512 / 8 = 64$) (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 5).

question: What are the three ways multi-head attention is used in the Transformer?
ground_truth: Encoder-decoder attention (queries from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder output), encoder self-attention, and decoder self-attention (masked to prevent leftward information flow).
answer:
The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three distinct ways (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 5):

Encoder-Decoder Attention Layers: The queries come from the previous decoder layer, while the keys and values come from the output of the encoder. This allows every position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the input sequence.
Encoder Self-Attention Layers: All keys, values, and queries come from the same place—the output of the previous layer in the encoder—allowing each position in the encoder to attend to all positions in the previous encoder layer.
Decoder Self-Attention Layers: Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position to attend to all positions in the decoder up to that point. Masking is used to prevent leftward information flow and preserve the auto-regressive property.

question: Why did the authors choose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones?
ground_truth: Results were nearly identical, and the sinusoidal version may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training.
answer:
The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned positional embeddings primarily because:

Extrapolation: They hypothesized that the sinusoidal version might allow the model to generalize and extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).
Relative Position Attention: The sinusoidal functions allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, as any fixed offset $k$ can be represented as a linear function of the encoding at position $pos$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).

When they actually experimented with learned positional embeddings, both versions produced nearly identical results in performance (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).

question: Under what condition is a self-attention layer faster than a recurrent layer?
ground_truth: When the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d.
answer:
A self-attention layer is faster than a recurrent layer when the sequence length ($n$) is smaller than the representation dimensionality ($d$) (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7).

Here is why:

Computational Complexity: A self-attention layer has a per-layer complexity of $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, whereas a recurrent layer has a complexity of $O(n \cdot d^2)$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6). When $n < d$, self-attention requires fewer total computational operations.
Parallelization: Self-attention requires only $O(1)$ sequential operations (making it highly parallelizable), compared to $O(n)$ sequential operations for a recurrent layer (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 6).

This condition ($n < d$) is typically met in state-of-the-art machine translation models that use word-piece or byte-pair representations (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7). For extremely long sequences where $n$ exceeds $d$, models can alternatively use restricted self-attention to maintain computational efficiency (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7).

question: What optimizer and hyperparameters were used?
ground_truth: Adam with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98, epsilon = 10^-9, and warmup_steps = 4000 with a learning rate that rises linearly then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number.
answer:
The Transformer model uses the Adam optimizer along with a custom learning rate schedule and several regularization hyperparameters (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7-8):

Optimizer Settings
Optimizer: Adam ($\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.98$, and $\epsilon = 10^{-9}$) (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7)
Learning Rate Schedule: The learning rate varied over the course of training according to the formula: $$\text{lrate} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(\text{step_num}^{-0.5}, \text{step_num} \cdot \text{warmup_steps}^{-1.5})$$ This increases the learning rate linearly for the first 4,000 warmup steps ($\text{warmup_steps} = 4000$) and decreases it thereafter proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7).
Regularization Hyperparameters
Residual Dropout: Applied to the output of each sub-layer (before addition and normalization) as well as the sums of embeddings and positional encodings (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7–8):
Base model rate: $P_{\text{drop}} = 0.1$ (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 8)
Big model rate: $P_{\text{drop}} = 0.3$ (except for the English-to-French big model, which used $0.1$) (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 8, 9)
Label Smoothing: $\epsilon_{\text{ls}} = 0.1$ was employed during training (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 8).

question: What peak learning rate value was reached at the end of warmup?
answer:
Based on the paper, the learning rate schedule is given by the formula (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, p. 7):

$$\text{lrate} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(\text{step_num}^{-0.5}, \text{step_num} \cdot \text{warmup_steps}^{-1.5})$$

At the end of warmup ($\text{step_num} = \text{warmup_steps} = 4000$), the two terms in the minimum function are equal, yielding:

$$\text{lrate} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot 4000^{-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{512} \times 4000} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-5}$$

(using $d_{\text{model}} = 512$) (b9b2ae42-Attention.pdf, pp. 5, 7)
